In 1974 a well-known book linked the Arab oil crisis to Armageddon; it was revised in 1990 for the Gulf crisis and again in 2007.
Many 1970s books named the Soviet Union as Ezekiel's Gog; the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

Futurists say Jesus told us to watch the signs and that the regathering of Israel in 1948 is a real marker. They agree some teachers overreach, but they hold that the general trend of events can fit the prophetic pattern.
Have earlier generations also believed they were the last?
Yes. From the Montanists in the 2nd century to Luther and the Russian Mennonite trek to Central Asia in the 1880s, many believers were sure the end was near. All were wrong.

The fulfilled reading uses history as a check on confidence. In the second century the Montanists expected the New Jerusalem to come down in Phrygia. In the twelfth century Joachim of Fiore taught that a new age would begin around 1260. Martin Luther thought the last day was very close. In 1880-1884 groups of Mennonites in Russia made a "Great Trek" east to meet the Lord. Many nineteenth-century writers felt the same. Each group read the signs of its day. Each was sincere and each was mistaken. This pattern does not prove that Christ will never return. It shows that feeling "we are the last generation" is not evidence. Jesus said the day and hour are unknown.
The Mennonite trek led by Claas Epp Jr. expected Christ's return in 1889 in Central Asia.
Joachim of Fiore (about 1135-1202) divided history into three ages and expected a new age about 1260.

Futurists accept that past date-setting failed but argue that one generation will be right, and that unique modern markers (Israel since 1948, global technology) make our time different. Others reply that every generation saw its own markers as unique.
Why did the Reformers and the Westminster Confession call the pope the Antichrist?

They saw a corrupt church claiming Christ's headship and persecuting the gospel. They read 2 Thessalonians 2 as describing that power. History shows how each age reads prophecy through its own troubles.

The fulfilled reading treats this as an example of reading prophecy through present pain. In the late Middle Ages the church claimed power over kings and souls. Many leaders lived openly in sin, and reformers were burned. Luther, Calvin and many others concluded that the papacy was the "man of sin" who sits in God's temple. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 25.6) says the pope is that Antichrist. These men loved Scripture and had real reasons for their view. Yet many Protestant churches later revised or dropped the statement, for example the American Presbyterian revision of 1903. The lesson is that sincere and gifted believers can be wrong when they identify the beast with the powers of their own day.
Westminster Confession 25.6 calls the pope "that Antichrist, that man of sin".
The Presbyterian Church in the USA removed the clause in 1903.

Historicists still hold that the papacy fits the beast and the man of sin over many centuries. Futurists look for one person at the end. Preterists see first-century figures, such as Nero or Jewish rebel leaders. Catholic writers reject the charge entirely.
Did the Black Death and the Hundred Years' War mean the end had come?
No. Plague, war and church corruption made the 1300s seem like the end. Many said so, using the same verses used today, but history went on.

On the fulfilled reading, the fourteenth century is a strong test case. The plague reached Constantinople in 1347 and England in 1348. It killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people. Courts closed, crops rotted and the dead lay unburied. At the same time England and France fought the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453). The church was weak and divided, and from 1378 there were two rival popes. Preachers used Matthew 24 and Revelation to say the end was at hand. John Wycliffe rightly saw the greed and sin of the clergy. But the world did not end. Wars, plagues and famines are part of a fallen world, and Jesus said such things do not mean the end is yet.
The Black Death spread along trade routes from Central Asia to Europe in 1346-1351.
The Western Schism (1378-1417) saw two and later three rival popes.

Futurists agree that past crises were not the end but say they were "birth pains" that foreshadow a final, greater fulfilment. Historicists may see the plague years as part of the seals or trumpets of Revelation.
Can a preacher be right about the sins of his age and still wrong about the end?
Yes. John Wycliffe rightly condemned the greed of the clergy, but the late 1300s were not the last days. Moral diagnosis is not a prophetic timetable.

The fulfilled reading separates two things that are often joined. A preacher may see clearly that his society is sick. That is the work of a prophet in the moral sense, like Amos against Israel. But to say, "Therefore the end of the world is here," is a different claim that needs a clear word from God. John Wycliffe (died 1384) blamed the corruption of the church for God's judgment through plague. He was right about the sin. Yet the world continued for centuries. Paul told Timothy that evil people would go from bad to worse, and he also said their folly would become plain to all. Evil in any age calls for repentance. It does not by itself date the return of Christ.
Amos condemned Israel's injustice around 760 BC; judgment came through Assyria in 722 BC, not the end of the world.
Wycliffe's followers, the Lollards, carried his moral critique forward for over a century.

Many futurists agree, and say moral decline is a general sign rather than a timetable. Others say 2 Timothy 3 describes a final, worldwide decline before the end, so moral collapse is a valid clue in every age.
Does great upheaval in our nation prove that Jesus will return in our generation?
No. Even the worst crisis in history would not show that the end is near. The Bible gives no rule that national trouble dates Christ's coming.

Read covenantally, the "near" events of the New Testament were tied to one covenant people and one city. They were not tied to any modern nation. A country could go through war, collapse or plague without any of it being a sign of the end. Jesus told his disciples not to be alarmed by wars and rumours, because "the end is not yet". The church has lived through the fall of Rome, the Mongol invasions, the plague, two world wars and nuclear threat. Each seemed final. Christians are called to faithfulness in every season. They pray, serve and build. They do not need to tie their hope to the latest crisis, because their hope rests on Christ's promises, not on reading the times.
In 1914 some teachers taught that the First World War would lead straight to Armageddon.
Daniel 2:21 says God changes times and seasons and removes kings; upheaval is under his rule, not a countdown.

Futurists answer that national troubles alone are not proof, but the convergence of many signs at once, especially around Israel, points to a near end. Historicists see major upheavals as landmarks on the prophetic timeline.
Why have Christians in every age pointed to wars, earthquakes and plagues as signs of the end?
These things happen in every generation, so every generation can find them. Tertullian in the 2nd century and Gregory the Great in the 6th both did so.

The fulfilled reading observes that the "signs" most often quoted are constant features of a fallen world. About AD 197 Tertullian wrote of terrible wars, plagues, famines and earthquakes in history. Around 601, Pope Gregory the Great wrote to King Ethelbert of Kent that some signs of the end were already happening, and others would soon follow. Each writer saw his own troubles as unique. Jesus listed such events in Matthew 24:6-8, but he called them only "the beginning of birth pains" and said "the end is not yet". On the fulfilled reading, those signs came in the decades before AD 70: famine under Claudius, earthquakes in Asia and Judea, and wars across the empire. They were signs for that generation.
Gregory's letter to Ethelbert is preserved in Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.32.
Acts 11:28 records the famine under Claudius (about AD 46-48).
An earthquake struck Laodicea in AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27).

Futurists accept that such events are common but argue Jesus spoke of their increase in frequency and intensity, like birth pains, at the end. Others note measured earthquakes have not clearly increased, so they focus on the combination of signs instead.
Why do disaster and hope of a coming millennium so often go together?
When the known world seems to collapse, people grasp at promises of sudden rescue. Leaders have used that fear to stir up followers.

The fulfilled reading draws on the study of history. Scholars of popular movements have shown that hope of a sudden new age grows strongest in times of disaster. When plague, war or famine destroy normal life, people become open to ideas they would once have rejected. Some leaders have used this to agitate the faithful. Others turned it into revolution, promising a purified society. In 1534-1535 radical Anabaptists seized the city of Münster in Germany, declared it the New Jerusalem, and the result was violence and death. Scripture calls believers to a different hope: a kingdom that grows like a mustard seed and like yeast, through the gospel, not through panic or the sword.
The Münster rebellion (1534-1535) ended with the city recaptured and its leaders executed.
Norman Cohn, The Pursuit of the Millennium (1957), traces such movements in medieval Europe.

Most Christians of every view reject violent end-time movements. Premillennialists note that their hope is for Christ to bring the kingdom, not people, so it should make believers less, not more, revolutionary. Scholars see these patterns across many religions.
When a preacher says Armageddon is "near", what should "near" mean?
In the Bible, "near" meant near for the first readers. Revelation said its events were near and must soon take place for the seven churches.

On the fulfilled reading, the word "near" must be read the same way in every place. Revelation opens and closes by saying its events "must shortly take place" and "the time is near" (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:6, 10). Those words were written to seven real churches in Asia. If "near" can stretch to two thousand years, it no longer means anything. Many preachers today say that Armageddon is near without explaining what they mean. The preterist reading holds that Revelation was written before AD 70, under Nero, and that its main judgments fell within the lifetime of its first readers. Then "near" means near. The date of Revelation is debated, but the time words are clear either way.
Daniel was told to seal his vision because it was for "many days" ahead (Daniel 8:26); John was told not to seal his (Revelation 22:10).
Many preterists date Revelation to about AD 65-68, during or soon after Nero's persecution.

Most scholars date Revelation to about AD 95 under Domitian, citing Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3). Futurists say "near" means "next on God's calendar" or that "shortly" means "suddenly". Idealists say the time is always near because every age faces the same conflict.
Who were the Montanists, and what happened to their prophecy?
Montanus and two prophetesses in 2nd-century Phrygia claimed to speak for the Holy Spirit and said the New Jerusalem would soon come down. It did not.

The fulfilled reading uses the Montanists as an early warning. Around AD 160-170 in Phrygia, in modern Turkey, a new convert named Montanus began to prophesy in ecstatic speech. Two women, Prisca and Maximilla, joined him. They claimed to be the voice of the Paraclete, the Spirit promised in John 14. They said the New Jerusalem would descend at the village of Pepuza. Maximilla said that after her there would be no more prophecy, only the end. She died around AD 179, and the end did not come. The church judged the movement by its fruit and its failed words. The apostle John had already told believers to test the spirits.
Eusebius, Church History 5.16-18, preserves early reports on the Montanists.
Tertullian joined the Montanist movement late in life, showing how attractive it could be.

Some historians think the Montanists were mainly a renewal movement seeking stricter discipline, and that their opponents exaggerated their claims. Charismatic Christians today sometimes see them as a warning against both false prophecy and the quenching of true gifts.
Did the fall of Rome, the Inquisition or the Black Death bring the end?
No. Christians saw each as the beginning of the end, yet the world continued. Note: Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in AD 410 and by the Vandals in AD 455.

The fulfilled reading lists these crises to show a pattern. When Alaric and the Visigoths sacked Rome in AD 410, many thought the world was ending. Augustine wrote The City of God partly to answer that fear: earthly cities fall, but God's city remains. In the 1200s, church courts against heresy brought terror to many, and some saw this as the last days. In 1347-1350 the Black Death killed millions. The writer Boccaccio described how law and order broke down. Some people gave up all restraint because they thought their days were numbered. Fear of the end did not make them holy. Each crisis passed, and the gospel went on. The New Testament calls believers to steady faithfulness.
Augustine began The City of God about AD 413, after the sack of Rome.
Boccaccio's Decameron (about 1353) opens with a description of the plague in Florence in 1348.

Futurists agree these were not the end but describe them as types or foreshadowings. Historicists sometimes link the fall of Rome to the trumpets of Revelation 8-9. All views agree that crisis alone is not proof of the end.
What did Martin Luther believe about the end?
Luther said no one knows the date, yet he was sure the end was very near. In 1532 he wrote that the last day was at hand.

The fulfilled reading uses Luther to show that even great teachers can misjudge timing. Luther often said that Christians know the day of Christ's return no more than an unborn baby knows the day of its birth. Yet he was convinced that the last day was close. In 1532 he wrote that his calendar had run out and he saw nothing more in Scripture. He saw the papacy and the Turkish armies at Vienna (1529) as the final enemies. Luther's great gift was the gospel of grace. On timing, he shared the anxiety of his age. Almost five hundred years later, the lesson is to hold to Jesus' words: the day and hour are not given.
The Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1529 shaped Luther's view of the Turks as an end-time enemy.
Luther died in 1546; the church has lived nearly five centuries since.

Lutheran and Reformed writers note that Luther's urgency was pastoral, calling people to readiness. Futurists say Luther was right in principle to live expecting Christ, only wrong on the timing. Historicists share much of his reading of the papacy.
How did year-day calculations shape predictions from the 1790s to the 1840s?
Interpreters treated prophetic days as years. They said the 1,260 days ended about 1798 and the 2,300 days of Daniel 8:14 ended about 1843-1844.

The fulfilled reading treats this era as a lesson in method. After the French Revolution, many respected scholars and pastors in Britain and America counted each prophetic "day" as a year. They said the 1,260 days of Revelation 12:6 had ended, often in 1798, when French troops took the pope captive. Others focused on the 2,300 "evenings and mornings" of Daniel 8:14 and the cleansing of the sanctuary. William Miller calculated that this pointed to about 1843, later fixed as 22 October 1844. Thousands waited, and nothing happened. The day became known as the Great Disappointment. Biblical numbers in prophecy are real, but they belong to their own setting. Daniel 8 itself links the 2,300 to the little horn, widely identified with Antiochus IV (167-164 BC).
Pope Pius VI was taken prisoner by French forces in February 1798.
The Maccabees cleansed the temple in December 164 BC, celebrated at Hanukkah (1 Maccabees 4:52-59).

Historicists still use the year-day principle, citing Numbers 14:34 and Ezekiel 4:6. Seventh-day Adventists reinterpret 1844 as the start of Christ's heavenly work of judgment. Futurists read the days as literal days in a future tribulation.
Was there an end-of-the-world panic at the year 1000?
Popular stories say crowds filled St. Peter's in Rome expecting the end. Historians debate how widespread the fear was, but end-time hopes did rise around 1000 and 1033.

The fulfilled reading cites the year 1000 as one more date that passed. Later writers described weeping crowds in Rome and people giving away land before the end. Modern historians disagree on how much of this is legend. Some, such as Richard Landes, argue that real anxiety rose around AD 1000 and again around 1033, a thousand years after the cross. Others say the panic stories were invented centuries later. Either way, the expectations failed. Similar hopes gathered around 1100, 1200 and 1260, and later teachers named 1533, 1734 and other years. A date tied to a round number has no support in Scripture. The thousand years of Revelation 20 is about the reign of Christ, not a calendar trigger.
Melchior Hoffman announced Christ's return for 1533 in Strasbourg.
Nicholas of Cusa (1401-1464) speculated the world would not last beyond the early 1700s.

Medieval historians remain divided. Some premillennial writers see the "day as a thousand years" pattern (a six-thousand-year history) as a valid clue, an idea found in early writers like the Epistle of Barnabas. Most scholars now treat such schemes as speculation.
What happened with the predictions of a rapture in 1988?
Many taught that Israel's rebirth in 1948 plus a forty-year generation pointed to 1988. One book gave 88 reasons. It failed, and then failed again with new dates.

On the fulfilled reading, 1988 shows what happens when "this generation" is moved from the first century to the twentieth. Popular teaching made Israel's statehood in 1948 the fig tree of Matthew 24:32. A biblical generation was counted as forty years. So 1988 seemed to be the year. Edgar Whisenant published 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988 and claimed he could not be wrong unless the Bible was wrong. After the September date passed, he said he was off by one year, then made more dates. Other groups also set dates; some young men even claimed to be the two witnesses of Revelation 11. Jesus actually tied the fig tree lesson to his own generation.
Whisenant's booklet was widely mailed; millions of copies circulated in 1988.
His follow-up, The Final Shout: Rapture Report 1989, moved the date to 1989.

Most dispensational leaders rejected Whisenant's date-setting at the time. Some still see 1948 as prophetically significant but avoid fixed dates. Others say a "generation" may be 70 or 80 years (Psalms 90:10), which moves the window.
Did Jesus stop reading Isaiah 61:2 to show that "the day of vengeance" was postponed two thousand years?
No. Jesus himself later said the "days of vengeance" would fall on Jerusalem within his generation (Luke 21:22, 32).

On the fulfilled reading, the theory reads too much into a pause. In Nazareth, Jesus read Isaiah 61:1-2 and stopped before "the day of vengeance of our God" (Luke 4:18-19). Some writers built a timetable on this, adding exactly 2,000 "biblical years" of 360 days to reach AD 2000. But nothing in the New Testament says the vengeance was postponed. Later in Luke, Jesus said Jerusalem would be surrounded by armies, for "these are days of vengeance" to fulfil all that is written. He added that "this generation" would not pass before all took place. So the day of vengeance was future to his hearers in Nazareth but came within forty years, in AD 70. The rejection of the Messiah set the stage.
Luke 21:20-22: armies around Jerusalem mark the "days of vengeance".
Roman legions under Titus surrounded Jerusalem in spring AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 5.2).

Many futurists say the pause shows a gap between the first and second comings, without fixing a date, and see AD 70 as a partial fulfilment of a final day of vengeance. They regard the 360-day calculation as one writer's speculation.
When God sets a timetable, how does he make it known?
He states it plainly: seven years of famine, forty years in the wilderness, seventy years of exile, four hundred years in Egypt. No hidden code is needed.

The fulfilled reading notes that biblical time periods are given openly to the people they concern. Joseph told Pharaoh there would be seven years of plenty and seven of famine. God told Israel they would wander forty years, one year for each day of spying. Jeremiah said Judah would serve Babylon seventy years, and Daniel later read that number in Jeremiah and prayed. God told Abraham his descendants would be afflicted four hundred years. None of these required secret math or calendar adjustments. Schemes that rest on hidden dates, jubilee cycles or the exact length of a year go beyond what God has said. The Bible's timetables are meant to be understood by ordinary believers.
Daniel 9:2: Daniel understood "from the books" the seventy years spoken through Jeremiah.
The first exiles were taken in 605 BC; Cyrus's decree came in 538 BC, close to seventy years.

Some futurists and historicists hold that God also hides patterns in numbers for the wise to find (Daniel 12:9-10). Most scholars agree, however, that Scripture never invites fixing the date of Christ's return.
Why did the Gulf War of 1990-1991 bring a new wave of prophecy books?
Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and the focus on Babylon led writers to revive and revise older books. When events moved on, the books lost their force.

The fulfilled reading sees this as newspaper exegesis on a large scale. When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, old prophecy books were rushed back into print. One popular title on oil and Armageddon was revised to fit new events. Another book argued that Saddam Hussein's rebuilding of ancient Babylon was the start of end-time prophecy. Even fellow futurists disagreed, noting that Babylon remained a ruin. Within a few years these books were sold off cheaply. The Bible's "Babylon" in Revelation is described as the city where the Lord was crucified and the blood of the prophets was shed. On the preterist reading, that points to first-century Jerusalem, not a modern Iraq.
Revelation 11:8 calls the great city the place "where our Lord was crucified".
Saddam Hussein began rebuilding parts of ancient Babylon in the 1980s; the work stopped after 1990.

Some futurists still expect a literal rebuilt Babylon in Iraq. Others see Babylon as Rome or as a world system. Historicists often identify it with papal Rome. Idealists see it as the seductive world in every age.
What do the 1992 and 1994 rapture dates teach us?
A Korean group named 28 October 1992; a radio Bible teacher named September 1994 and later 2011. All failed, and the leaders said they had simply misread God.

The fulfilled reading sees the same pattern repeating. In South Korea, a movement placed newspaper notices that the rapture would happen on 28 October 1992. Many followers gave up jobs and homes. When the night passed, a leader said they had got the message wrong. In the same year a newsletter editor wrote that his summer issue would probably be his last. Harold Camping, an American radio teacher, calculated that Christ would come in 1994, building on unproven dates such as the creation of Adam in 11,013 BC. He later named 21 May 2011. God's message is not hidden in such calculations. It is in Scripture, and Scripture said the coming in judgment was near for the first-century church.
Korean police were present at many churches on the night of 28 October 1992 to prevent harm.
Camping's 21 May 2011 prediction drew worldwide attention and then failed; he later apologised.

All major Christian traditions rejected these date-setters. Futurists say the failure of false dates does not disprove a future rapture, only careless teachers. Critics of the faith use them to mock all belief in Christ's return.
What lessons do the Waco and Ruby Ridge tragedies teach about end-time teaching?
Groups convinced that Revelation's judgments were about to break on them read government action as the beast. Fear and misreading helped produce deadly results.

The fulfilled reading draws a sober lesson. At Waco, Texas, in 1993, the Branch Davidian leader David Koresh taught that only he could open the seven seals of Revelation. During a 51-day standoff he spoke of the end being fulfilled. On 19 April 1993 the compound burned, and about 76 people died, including many children. At Ruby Ridge, Idaho, in 1992, a family shaped partly by popular prophecy books believed the government was the beast and fled to the mountains. A shoot-out left three dead. Government actions in both cases are widely criticised. Still, the teaching that Revelation's judgments were about to fall on them deepened fear and isolation. The fulfilled reading holds that those judgments belonged to the first century.
The Waco siege lasted from 28 February to 19 April 1993.
Revelation 5:5 says only the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Christ, can open the scroll.

Futurist leaders strongly reject such cults and note that Koresh distorted their teaching. They argue false teachers can misuse any view. Many observers also blame government handling of both sieges. Scholars warn that any view that names present enemies as the beast can feed fear.
What harm comes from repeated cries that "the end is near"?
Like the boy who cried wolf, the church loses credibility. Unbelievers ask why they should trust preachers who have been wrong for centuries.

The fulfilled reading uses Aesop's fable as a picture. A shepherd boy cried "Wolf!" for fun. The villagers came twice and found nothing. When a wolf really came, no one listened, and the flock was lost. In the same way, false alarms about the end harm the sheep. Many preachers have used the soon return of Jesus to urge decisions for Christ. But if they are wrong again and again, listeners may ask why they should believe anything else these preachers say. Some conclude the whole Christian message is false. God promised shepherds who would feed his people with knowledge and understanding, not with the latest headline. Faithful teaching keeps both the hope of Christ's return and honesty about time.
Jeremiah 3:15: God promises shepherds after his own heart who feed with knowledge.
Skeptical writers regularly list failed Christian end-time dates as evidence against the Bible.
Futurists agree date-setting harms the church, but most deny they set dates. They argue that urging readiness for an any-moment return is biblical, and that the abuse of a truth does not cancel it.
When the New Testament says the end is "at hand", at hand for whom?
For the first readers. Peter told his readers to be sober because the end of all things was at hand. Read plainly, this meant their own time.

On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament does use the nearness of Christ's coming to urge believers on. But the near judgment was the fall of Jerusalem and the old covenant order in AD 70. Peter wrote, "The end of all things is at hand; therefore be sober and pray" (1 Peter 4:7). The command to be sober and pray was for his readers, so the nearness was theirs too. Jesus told his disciples to pray that they might escape "all these things that will come to pass" (Luke 21:36). John wrote, "It is the last hour" (1 John 2:18). If words have meaning, these writers spoke of their own day. Taking God at his word means accepting this, even against popular teaching.
Christians in Jerusalem fled to Pella before the siege, according to Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3.
The temple worship that defined the old order ended permanently in AD 70.

Futurists and many amillennialists say "at hand" means the end is the next great event, so believers in every age must be ready. Some scholars see "prophetic foreshortening": near and far events seen together, like mountain peaks from a distance.
What do all the failed end-time predictions have in common?
The predictors were sure, and they were wrong. They also moved Bible texts out of their first-century setting and applied them to their own time.

The fulfilled reading sums up two thousand years of date-setting this way. One historian has catalogued more than a thousand failed predictions, from names of the Antichrist to dates for Christ's return. Two marks run through nearly all of them. First, the predictors were certain. Second, they were mistaken. A third mark is common too: they took prophecies meant for the first generation and applied them to their own news. The historian Mark Noll warned that those who predict details and dates should remember how many before them misread the signs. Scripture tells us that secret things belong to God, while revealed things belong to us. Humility about the unknown and confidence in the revealed is the healthy path.
Mark Noll, "Misreading the Signs of the Times", Christianity Today (6 February 1987).
Many 20th-century writers named Mussolini, Hitler, Stalin or Kissinger as possible Antichrists.

Futurists accept the warning against date-setting but say that naming possible signs without fixing dates is different. Historicists say past interpreters were often right about the general sweep, if not the dates. All agree humility is needed.
Why do new prophecy books appear every time war or disaster strikes?
Each crisis is read as proof of the end. Writers rarely check the history of earlier failed predictions or the first-century setting of the texts.

The fulfilled reading sees a repeating cycle. Missiles fall on the Middle East, a flood or earthquake strikes, and books predicting the end are rushed into print. After floods in the American Midwest in 1993, a pastor said the Bible's latter-day earthquakes meant all natural disasters, and that we lived in such a time. In 1980 a best seller promised that "we are the generation" that would see the end. Such claims ignore that Jesus' signs were given to his disciples about their own city and temple. They also ignore earlier writers who were just as sure. Scripture tells us to learn from history. The things that happened to Israel were written for our instruction, not as a mirror for every new headline.
